Nestling Western sandpipers (Calidris mauri) typically hatch from eggs incubated for a period of 18 to 22 days [ab = 18 to 22 days] under natural conditions, with optimal incubation temperatures measured at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these precocial chicks emerge at a wet weight of roughly 7.5 grams [Ww0 = roughly 7.5 grams], reflecting a modest initial body mass that is characteristic of small calidridine sandpipers. The actual mass at birth, measured immediately after the down dries, is approximately 5 grams [Wwb = approximately 5 grams], a value that represents the neonate's mass after complete yolk absorption. This initial mass is substantially lower than the ultimate adult body masses achieved later in life, highlighting the remarkable growth trajectory this species undergoes during its first few weeks of development. The incubation duration itself is consistent with values reported for other Arctic-breeding shorebirds, where thermal constraints in high-latitude nesting environments can prolong embryonic development compared to temperate congeners.

Once hatched, the chicks enter a rapid growth phase that culminates in fledging and nutritional independence. Under the metabolically active body temperatures typical of this species (approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is documented as 19 days [tx = 19 days], a developmental milestone marked by the achievement of sustained flight and the chick's departure from the natal territory. This brief fledging period is notably short compared to larger shorebird species, reflecting an adaptive strategy that minimizes the window of vulnerability to predators on the tundra breeding grounds. The ability to fly at such a young age, typically before the chick has reached its full adult mass, allows the juvenile to disperse to foraging sites where prey availability is higher. Field observations indicate that fledging success is strongly influenced by local food abundance during the nestling period, with chicks from broods hatched during peak insect emergence achieving this milestone more consistently than those from later clutches.

The period of juvenile development bridges the gap between fledging and the attainment of full adult body size. The ultimate wet weight for adult females of this sexually dimorphic species reaches approximately 31 grams [Wwi = approximately 31 grams], whereas males, which are the smaller sex, achieve a maximum adult body mass of about 28 grams [Wwi = about 28 grams]. This difference in mass, a difference of roughly three grams on average, is a consistent feature across populations and is linked to the distinct reproductive roles of each sex. Females, which invest heavily in egg production prior to incubation, carry a larger body frame that supports the energetic demands of clutch formation. Males, by contrast, tend to be more agile and may benefit energetically from a lighter body mass during the extended period of brood care they perform. These asymptotic masses are reached gradually over the first year of life, with most individuals attaining their adult body dimensions by their first spring migration.

Puberty in the Western sandpiper occurs well after the juvenile plumage has been replaced, and it marks the onset of gonadal development under the permissive thermal conditions of the breeding season. At a body temperature approximating 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 57 days [tp = 57 days], indicating that individuals can become reproductively competent within their first summer of life. This rapid sexual maturation, unusual among small calidridine sandpipers that typically defer reproduction, allows early-hatched juveniles to potentially breed during the same calendar year if conditions are favorable. However, the first successful clutch is rarely laid in the hatch year, as the energetic demands of completing somatic growth and gaining sufficient lipid reserves for migration typically take precedence. The onset of gonadal activity is marked by a surge in circulating testosterone levels in males and the commencement of ovarian follicle development in females, processes that are tightly synchronized with the photoperiodic cues of the subarctic summer.

First breeding for most Western sandpipers occurs considerably later than the initial attainment of sexual competence under standard thermal conditions of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. The time since birth at first brood is estimated at approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days], meaning that the majority of individuals do not produce their first successful clutch until their second calendar year of life, after returning from their first wintering grounds. at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]This two-year delay is typical for many Arctic-breeding sandpipers of the family Scolopacidae and reflects the lengthy migration distances these birds undertake, as well as the time required to establish a breeding territory and secure a mate. The annual reproductive output per pair is modest, with females depositing exactly four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = four eggs per clutch] in a single nesting attempt each season [F_R_i = single nesting attempt each season]. This fixed clutch size of four, remarkably consistent across the species' range, is an evolutionary adaptation to the energetic constraints of high-latitude breeding, where a five-egg clutch would impose unsustainable demands on provisioning parents. At 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for individuals in the wild reaches approximately 9.2 years [am = approximately 9.2 years], a relatively long duration for a charadriiform shorebird of this body size, which underscores the species' ability to navigate the hazards of long-distance migration across multiple years.
